# Conics and Pole-Polar Duality

## Definition and Existence of Conics

::: {#lem-pascalcond}
Let $A,B,C,D,E,F$ be points such that no three of them are collinear, then
$$
A(B,D;E,F)=C(B,D;E,F)
$$
if and only if 
$$P=AB\cap DE,\,Q=BC\cap EF,\,R=CD\cap FA$$ 
are collinear.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Since
$$
A(B,D;E,F)=(P,D;E,AF\cap DE),\,\,C(B,D;E,F)=(Q,CD\cap EF;E,F)
$$
we see that
$$
A(B,D;E,F)=C(B,D;E,F)\iff(P,D;E,AF\cap DE)=(Q,CD\cap EF;E,F)
$$
This is equivalent to $PQ,CD,AF$ being concurrent, i.e. $P,Q,R$ are collinear.
:::

In @lem-pascalcond, the points $P,Q,R$ are the intersections of the three pairs of opposite sides of the hexagon $ABCDEF$, so by symmetry this is equivalent to $B(A,C;E,F)=D(A,C;E,F)$. In conclusion, if two points among the six can be chosen so that the cross ratio of the remaining four points from each of them is the same, then this holds for any choice of two points among them. That is, the relation among these six points is symmetric. We temporarily call this relation the Pascal condition.

::: {#lem-pascaltrans}
Let $A,B,C,D,E,F,G$ be points such that no three of them are collinear. Suppose that $ABCDEF$ and $ABCDEG$ satisfy the Pascal condition, then $ABCDFG$ also satisfies the Pascal condition.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Consider the projective map
$$
f:\mathbb{L}_A\to\mathbb{L}_B,\,f(AC)=BC,\, f(AD)=BD,\, f(AE)=BE
$$
From the Pascal condition of $ABCDEF$ and $ABCDEG$, $f(AF)=BF$, $f(AG)=BG$, so $ABCDFG$ satisfies the Pascal condition.
:::

From this we construct a subset of $\mathbb{P}$ such that any six-point subset satisfies the Pascal condition.

::: {#lem-steinerconstruct}
Given distinct points $A,B$ and a projective map $f:\mathbb{L}_A\to\mathbb{L}_B$ such that $f(AB)\neq BA$, then any six-point subset of the set
$$
\{\ell\cap f(\ell)\mid \ell\in \mathbb{L}_A\}
$$ 
satisfies the Pascal condition (so no three points are collinear).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $\ell_i\cap f(\ell_i)=X_i$ where $i=1,\ldots,6$, and $X_i\neq A,B$. Since $f$ is projective, $A,X_i,X_j$ cannot be collinear where $i\neq j$ (similarly $B,X_i,X_j$ cannot be collinear). If $X_1,X_2,X_3$ are collinear, then
$$
A(X_1,X_2;X_3,B)=B(X_1,X_2;X_3,A)
$$
i.e. $f(AB)=BA$, contradiction. We conclude that no three points in the set are collinear.

Since $AX_1X_2X_3BX_4$ and $AX_1X_2X_3BX_5$ satisfy the Pascal condition, $AX_1X_2X_3X_4X_5$ also satisfies the Pascal condition. Analogously, $AX_1X_2X_3X_4X_6$ satisfies the Pascal condition, so from @lem-pascaltrans, $X_1X_2X_3X_4X_5X_6$ satisfies the Pascal condition.
:::

::: {#lem-tangentlem}
Let $A,B,C,D,E$ be points such that no three of them are collinear. Suppose that $\ell\in\mathbb{L}_A$ satisfies
$$
(AC,AD;AE,\ell)=B(C,D;E,A)
$$
then for any $F\neq A$ on $\ell$, $F(C,D;E,A)\neq B(C,D;E,A)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that $F\neq A\in \ell$ satisfies $F(C,D;E,A)= B(C,D;E,A)$, then $F(C,D;E,A)=A(C,D;E,F)$, i.e. $C,D,E$ are collinear by @thm-collinear, which is a contradiction.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
A non-empty set $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathbb{P}$ is said to be a (nondegenerate) **conic** if

(1) No three points in $\mathcal{C}$ are collinear.

(2) Any six-point set in $\mathcal{C}$ satisfies the Pascal condition.

(3) For any $P\in\mathcal{C}$, there exists a unique line $\ell$ through $P$ such that 
$$
\mathbb{P}_\ell\cap\mathcal{C}=\{P\}
$$
The line $\ell$ is called the **tangent** of $P$ to $\mathcal{C}$. This implies that any other line passing through $P$ passes through a second point on $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

Note that the construction in @lem-tangentlem implies the existence of the tangent $\ell$.

::: {#thm-conicexist}
Given $A,B,C,D,E$ (no three of which are collinear), there exists a unique (nondegenerate) conic $\mathcal{C}$ passing through the five points. This conic is denoted by $(ABCDE)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Consider the projective map
$$
f:\mathbb{L}_A\to\mathbb{L}_B,\,f(AC)=BC, \,f(AD)=BD,\, f(AE)=BE
$$
Suppose that $f(AB)=BA$, then @thm-collinear implies that $C,D,E$ are collinear, which is a contradiction.

From @lem-steinerconstruct, let $\mathcal{C}=\{\ell\cap f(\ell)\mid \ell\in \mathbb{L}_A\}$, then no three points in $\mathcal{C}$ are collinear, and any six-point set in $\mathcal{C}$ satisfies the Pascal condition. 

Let $P$ be a point on $\mathcal{C}$. Suppose that $\ell$ passes through $P$ such that $\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}$ intersect at exactly one point $P$, then we consider the projective map
$$
g:\mathbb{L}_P\to\mathbb{L}_A,\,g(PC)=AC,\, g(PD)=AD,\, g(PE)=AE
$$
Set $\ell\cap g(\ell)=X$, then $PACDEX$ satisfies the Pascal condition, and $ABCDEP$ satisfies the Pascal condition, so $ABCDEX$ satisfies the Pascal condition. We see that $X\in\mathcal{C}$, so $X=P$, i.e. $g(\ell)=AP$ and $\ell$ is unique. We conclude that $\mathcal{C}$ is a conic, and the uniqueness of $\mathcal{C}$ follows from this construction.
:::

We have established the existence of conics by construction. If six points lie on the same conic, they are said to be conconic.

::: {#thm-Pascal}
## Pascal theorem
Suppose that no three of $ABCDEF$ are collinear, then $ABCDEF$ are conconic if and only if 
$$AB\cap DE,\,BC\cap EF,\,CD\cap FA$$ 
are collinear.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This is the statement of @lem-pascalcond.
:::

When applying Pascal theorem, we usually say we apply it to the hexagon $ABCDEF$ (with the points labeled as in @thm-Pascal). Since Pascal theorem and the cross ratio condition are equivalent, we may apply Pascal theorem to the hexagon $AABCDE$ on the conic $(ABCDE)$. In this case, $AA$ is viewed as the tangent of $A$ to $(ABCDE)$.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
Note that Pappus theorem is the special case of Pascal theorem on two lines; or in @lem-steinerconstruct, when $f(AB)=BA$, the locus of all points $\ell\cap f(\ell)$ is the union of a line and $AB$. This suggests that we may view the union of two lines as a degenerate conic. In what follows, conics are assumed to be nondegenerate unless stated otherwise.
:::

## Cross Ratios, Projective Maps, and Involutions on Conics

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Define the cross ratio of points $A,B,C,D$ on $\mathcal{C}$ to be
$$
(A,B;C,D)_\mathcal{C}=P(A,B;C,D)
$$
where $P$ is an arbitrary point on $\mathcal{C}$ (the line $AA$ means the tangent at $A$). From the definition of conics and @lem-tangentlem, the value of the cross ratio does not depend on the choice of $P$.
:::

Conics are cross-ratio sets.

::: {#thm-steinerconic}
## Steiner conic
Let $P,Q$ be distinct points, $f:\mathbb{L}_P\to \mathbb{L}_Q$ be a projective map.

(1) If $f(PQ)=QP$, then there exists a line $m$ such that $\ell, f(\ell), m$ are concurrent for each $\ell\in\mathbb{L}_P$.

(2) If $f(PQ)\neq QP$, then the locus of $\ell\cap f(\ell)$ (where $\ell\in \mathbb{L}_P$) is a conic passing through $P,Q$.

Moreover, the function $\ell\mapsto \ell\cap f(\ell)$ is projective.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows from @thm-collinear and @lem-steinerconstruct.
:::

::: {#thm-projaxis}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic, $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$ be a projective map (that is not the identity), then there exists a unique line $\ell$ such that for each $X,Y\in \mathcal{C}$,
$$
Xf(Y)\cap Yf(X)\in\ell
$$
We call $\ell$ the **projective axis** of $f$. Note that the intersections of $\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are the fixed points of $f$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Fix $A\in\mathcal{C}$, consider the projective map
$$
g:\mathbb{L}_{f(A)}\to\mathbb{L}_A, \,f(A)X\mapsto X\mapsto f(X)\mapsto Af(X)
$$
Since $g(f(A)A)=Af(A)$, from Steiner conic, the locus of $f(A)X\cap Af(X)$ is a line $\ell$, i.e. for any $X,Y\in \mathcal{C}$,
$$
Af(X)\cap Xf(A),\,Af(Y)\cap Yf(A)\in\ell
$$
Apply Pascal theorem to the hexagon $Af(X)Yf(A)Xf(Y)$, $Xf(Y)\cap Yf(X)$ is also on $\ell$.
:::

::: {#lem-polar}
Let $P\notin\mathcal{C}$. For any point $X\in\mathcal{C}$, let $X'$ be the second intersection of $PX$ and $\mathcal{C}$, then

(1) There exists a unique line $\ell$ such that for any $X\in\mathcal{C}$, the harmonic conjugate $X_0$ of $P$ with respect to $X|X'$ is on $\ell$.

(2) The function $f:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C}, X\mapsto X'$ is an involution, and the projective axis of $f$ is $\ell$. The intersection of the tangents of $X,X'$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is on $\ell$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Fix points $A,B\in\mathcal{C}$ such that $P,A, B$ are not collinear, let $PA,PB$ intersect $\mathcal{C}$ again at $A',B'$, and the harmonic conjugates of $P$ with respect to $A|A'$ and $B|B'$ are $A_0,B_0$, respectively. From @thm-collinear, the points
$$
AB\cap A'B', \,AB'\cap A'B,\, A_0,\, B_0
$$
are collinear. Apply Desargues theorem to the triangles $ABX$ and $A'B'X'$, the points
$$
AB\cap A'B',\, BX\cap B'X',\, AX\cap A'X'
$$
are collinear. Apply Pascal theorem to the hexagon $BXAB'X'A'$, the points
$$
BX\cap B'X',\, AX\cap A'X',\, AB'\cap BA'
$$
are collinear. Let $A_0B_0=\ell$, then $\ell$ passes through $BX\cap B'X'$ from the three collinearities. Interchanging $X$ and $X'$, $BX'\cap B'X\in\ell$. From @thm-collinear, $B_0,\, BX\cap B'X',\, BX'\cap B'X,\,X_0$ are collinear on $\ell$, which proves (1).

Since $BX\cap B'X'\in\ell$, the function $f:X\mapsto X'=B'(BX\cap\ell)\cap\mathcal{C}$ is a projective map, which proves (2).
:::

::: {#cor-conicinvolution}
Let $f:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C}$ be a projective map, then $f$ is an involution if and only if $Xf(X)$ passes through a fixed point for all $X\in\mathcal{C}$. The fixed point is called the perspector of $f$.
:::

::: {#thm-twointersect}
Given a conic $\mathcal{C}$ and a point $P\notin \mathcal{C}$, there exist two lines through $P$ tangent to $\mathcal{C}$. Given a line $m$ not tangent to $\mathcal{C}$, then $m$ and $\mathcal{C}$ intersect at two points.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $f_P:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C}$ be the involution with perspector $P$. Let $P_1,P_2$ be the fixed points of $f_P$ (by @lem-invfix), then $PP_1,PP_2$ are the tangents.

Fix $R,S\in m$, let the tangency points of the two tangents of $R$ (resp. $S$) to $\mathcal{C}$ be $A,A'$ (resp. $B,B'$). Set $Q=AA'\cap BB'$. From @lem-polar, let $f_Q$ be the involution on $\mathcal{C}$ with perspector $Q$, then the projective axis of $f_Q$ is $m$, so the fixed points $Q_1,Q_2$ of $f_Q$ are the intersections of $m$ and $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

::: {#cor-harmonicquad}
Let $P_1,P_2,X,Y\in \mathcal{C}$, then $(P_1,P_2;X,Y)_\mathcal{C}=-1$ if and only if the intersection of the tangents of $P_1,P_2$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is on $XY$.
:::

Combining @thm-projaxis and @thm-twointersect, for any projective map $f:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C}$, there are $1$ (when the projective axis and $\mathcal{C}$ are tangent) or $2$ fixed points of $f$.

::: {#lem-uniquefixedpoint}
Given a conic $\mathcal{C}$ and a projective map $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$ that is not the identity, then the fixed points of $f$ are the intersections of the projective axis and $\mathcal{C}$ (there may be $1$ or $2$ fixed points). If $f$ has a unique fixed point $P$, then for all $X\in \mathcal{C}$,
$$
(P,f(X);X,f(f(X)))=-1
$$
This is true for any cross-ratio set.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let the tangent of $P$ to $\mathcal{C}$ be $\ell$, and set $Y=f(X)$, then $Xf(Y)\cap Yf(X)\in \ell$, i.e. $Xf(f(X))$ passes through the intersection of the tangents of $f(X),P$ to $\mathcal{C}$. The harmonicity follows from @cor-harmonicquad.

For any cross-ratio set $\mathscr{A}$ and a projective map $f:\mathscr{A}\to \mathscr{A}$, fix a projective map $g:\mathcal{C}\to\mathscr{A}$ and apply the conclusion on conics to $g^{-1}\circ f\circ g:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C}$.
:::

## Extension of Projective Maps Between Conics

We investigate the problem of extending projective maps to projective transformations.

::: {#thm-extension}
Given conics $\mathcal{C}_1, \mathcal{C}_2$ and a projective map $f:\mathcal{C}_1\to \mathcal{C}_2$, there exists a unique projective transformation $\rho$ such that for each $X\in\mathcal{C}_1$, $\rho(X)=f(X)$. The projective transformation $\rho$ is called the extension of $f$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Fix $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4\in\mathcal{C}_1$ and set $c=(X_1,X_2;X_3,X_4)_{\mathcal{C}_1}$. Let $\rho$ be the projective transformation satisfying $\rho(X_i)=f(X_i)$ for $i=1,2,3,4$ (so $\rho$ is unique). Note that
$$
\mathcal{C}_1=\{X\mid X(X_1,X_2;X_3,X_4)=c\}
$$
Applying $\rho$, $(f(X_1),f(X_2);f(X_3),f(X_4))_{\mathcal{C}_2}=c$, so
$$
\rho(\mathcal{C}_1)=\{Y\mid Y(f(X_1),f(X_2);f(X_3),f(X_4))=c\}=\mathcal{C}_2
$$
Since projective transformations preserve cross ratio, for all $X\in\mathcal{C}_1$, $\rho(X)=f(X)$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
Let $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$. In this case, there is another way to see the existence of the extension. Since $f$ is the composition of two involutions, without loss of generality, we may assume that $f$ is the involution with perspector $P$, and $\ell$ is the projective axis of $f$.

Given $A,B,C\in \mathcal{C}$, define $\rho$ to be the perspective transformation from $ABC$ to $f(A)f(B)f(C)$ (the perspector and perspectrix are $P$ and $\ell$, respectively). From @lem-polar and @lem-perspectivefix,
$$
(f(A),\rho(f(A));P,f(A)P\cap \ell)=-1=(A,\rho(A);P,AP\cap \ell)
$$
This implies that $\rho(f(A))=A$ and that $\rho$ is an involutive transformation (from the second equality), so $\rho(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{C}$ and $\rho(X)=f(X)$ for all $X\in\mathcal{C}$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
Suppose that $P_1,P_2$ are two distinct fixed points of the projective map $f:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C}$, and $\rho$ is the extension of $f$. Let $\ell_1,\ell_2$ be the tangents of $P_1,P_2$ to $\mathcal{C}$, respectively, then $\rho(\ell_1)$ is tangent to $\mathcal{C}$ at $\rho(P_1)=P_1$, i.e. $\rho(\ell_1)=\ell_1$, and similarly, $\rho(\ell_2)=\ell_2$. Let $P=\ell_1\cap \ell_2$, then $\rho(P)=P$, i.e. $P_1,P_2,P$ are the fixed points of $\rho$.
:::

::: {#lem-projfixlineintersection}
Let $\rho$ be a projective transformation with a fixed line $\ell$ (i.e. $\rho(\ell)=\ell$). Fix $P,Q\in \ell$, and for any point $X\in \mathbb{P}$, define
$$
\rho_1:X\mapsto PX\cap Q\rho(X)
$$
then $\rho_1$ is a projective transformation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $X$ vary on $m\neq\ell$, then $PX\mapsto Q\rho(X)$ is a projective map, and when $X=\ell\cap m$, $PX=Q\rho(X)$, so by Steiner conic,  the locus of $\rho_1(X)$ is a line, and $X\mapsto \rho_1(X)$ is projective, so $\rho_1$ preserves collinearity and cross ratio.
:::

Consider a projective map $f:\mathcal{C}_1\to \mathcal{C}_2$ and its extension $\rho$. Suppose that $PQ$ is a fixed line of $\rho$, then from @lem-projfixlineintersection, the locus of $PX\cap Q\rho(X)$ ($X\in\mathcal{C}_1$) is a conic. In particular, take $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$, then the projective axis of $f$ is a fixed line of $\rho$. From @lem-projfixlineintersection, we obtain the following corollary.

::: {#cor-projaxisconic}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic and $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$ be a projective map with projective axis $\ell$. Fix points $P,Q \in\ell$, then the locus of $PX\cap Qf(X)$ ($X\in \mathcal{C}$) is a conic.
:::

## Poles and Polars

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
In view of @thm-twointersect, for $P\in \mathcal{C}$, there are two tangents of $\mathcal{C}$ through $P$, each equal to the tangent at $P$ (i.e. the tangent is counted with multiplicity $2$); for $m$ tangent to $\mathcal{C}$, there are two intersections of $m$ and $\mathcal{C}$, each equal to the tangency point of $m$ with $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

Fix a conic $\mathcal{C}$. Under this definition, we may construct two tangents from any point to $\mathcal{C}$, and any line intersects $\mathcal{C}$ at two points.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic, $P$ be a point, and $m$ be a line.

(1) Suppose that the two tangents from $P$ to $\mathcal{C}$ are tangent to $\mathcal{C}$ at $P_1,P_2$. Define the **polar**  $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(P)$ of $P$ with respect to $\mathcal{C}$ to be the line $P_1P_2$.

(2) Suppose that $m$ and $\mathcal{C}$ intersect at $Q_1,Q_2$. Define the **pole** $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(m)$ of $m$ with respect to $\mathcal{C}$ to be the intersection of the tangents of $Q_1,Q_2$ to $\mathcal{C}$.

The transformation $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}$ is called the polar transformation, i.e. the maps $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}:\mathbb{P}\to \mathbb{L}$ and $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}:\mathbb{L}\to \mathbb{P}$. The composition $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}\circ \mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}$ is the identity.
:::

The polar of $P$ with respect to $\mathcal{C}$ is the line $\ell$ in @lem-polar. By definition, when $P\in\mathcal{C}$, then $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(P)$ is the tangent of $P$; when $m$ is tangent to $\mathcal{C}$, then $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(m)$ is the tangency point of $m$.

::: {#thm-lahire}
## La Hire
Let $A,B$ be points, and the line $AB$ intersect the conic $\mathcal{C}$ at $Q_1,Q_2$. The following are equivalent.

(1) The polar of $A$ passes through $B$.

(2) The polar of $B$ passes through $A$.

(3) $(A,B;Q_1,Q_2)=-1$.

In this case, $A,B$ are said to be **conjugate** with respect to $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
From @lem-polar, (1)$\iff$(3) and (2)$\iff$(3).
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
Suppose that $\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are not tangent, then $\mathcal{C}$ induces an involution on $\ell$ by 
$$
X\mapsto \ell\cap\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(X)
$$
The fixed points of the involution are the intersections of $\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Given a conic $\mathcal{C}$ and a triangle $ABC$. Suppose that any two of $A,B,C$ are conjugate with respect to $\mathcal{C}$, then $ABC$ is said to be a self-conjugate triangle (with respect to $\mathcal{C}$).
:::

::: {#thm-brocard}
## Brocard
Suppose that points $A,B,C,D$ are on a conic $\mathcal{C}$, then the three points
$$
AB\cap CD,\,AC\cap BD,\,AD\cap BC
$$
form a self-conjugate triangle with respect to $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $AB\cap CD=P$, then the polar of $P$ passes through the harmonic conjugates of $P$ with respect to $A|B$ and $C|D$. From @thm-collinear, the polar of $P$ passes through $AC\cap BD,AD\cap BC$.
:::

::: {#cor-brocardconj}
Let $A,B,C$ be points on a conic $\mathcal{C}$. For $X\in BC$, let $AB,\,AC$ meet $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(X)$ at $Y,Z$, then $Y,Z$ are conjugate.
:::

::: {#thm-polarproj}
Polar transformation preserves cross ratio: given a conic $\mathcal{C}$ and a line $\ell$ with pole $P$, the function
$$
f:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to\mathbb{L}_P,\,\,X\mapsto \mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(X)
$$
is a projective map (the inverse of $f$ is also projective).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
When $\ell$ is not tangent to $\mathcal{C}$, then $X\mapsto \ell\cap \mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(X)$ is an involution, i.e. 
$$
f:X\mapsto P(\ell\cap \mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(X))
$$ 
is projective. When $\ell$ is tangent to $\mathcal{C}$, we fix $A,B\in\mathcal{C}$, and let $XA,XB$ intersect $\mathcal{C}$ again at $X_A,X_B$. Consider the projective map
$$
g:\mathbb{L}_A\to \mathbb{L}_B,\,AX_B\mapsto BX_A
$$
By Steiner conic, the locus of $AX_B\cap BX_A$ is a conic through $P$. From Brocard theorem, 
$$
f:X\mapsto AX_B\cap BX_A\mapsto P(AX_B\cap BX_A)
$$
is projective.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Example.**
The composition $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}\circ \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}$ of the polar transformations with respect to two conics $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ is a projective transformation.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
Since five points determine a conic, there are at most $4$ intersections of two distinct conics. Assume that $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ intersect at four distinct points $A,\,B,\,C,\,D$, then the fixed points of $\rho=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}\circ \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}$ are exactly the points satisfying $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}$. From Brocard theorem, the vertices of the cevian triangle of $ABCD$ are the fixed points of $\rho$. This suggests that there is a close relation between the projective transformation $\rho$ and the intersection of conics.
:::

The polar transformation $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}$ interchanges points and lines, satisfies the relation
$$P\in m\iff \mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(m)\in \mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(P)
$$ 
and preserves cross ratio. This shows that polar transformations realize duality: to obtain the dual statement, we take the polar transformation of any conic.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
Consider all transformations $\mathfrak{p}$ that realize duality, i.e. $\mathfrak{p}$ consists of functions
$$
\mathfrak{p}:\mathbb{P}\to \mathbb{L}, \mathfrak{p}:\mathbb{L}\to \mathbb{P}
$$
such that
$$
P\in m\iff\mathfrak{p}(m)\in \mathfrak{p}(P)
$$
and that $\mathfrak{p}$ preserves cross ratio. In this case, $\mathfrak{p}$ is said to be a dual transformation. Similar to the case of projective transformations, a dual transformation is characterized by the value at four points (no three of which are collinear) by the same argument in @thm-projtransunique. Suppose that $\mathfrak{p}$ is some polar transformation, then $\mathfrak{p}\circ\mathfrak{p}(P)=P$, so it is clear that there exist dual transformations that are not polar transformations.
:::

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic. We will show that a triangle and its image under $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}$ are perspective.

::: {#thm-poleperspective}
Given a conic $\mathcal{C}$ and a triangle $ABC$, set 
$$
A_1=\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(BC),\,B_1=\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(CA),\,C_1=\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(AB)
$$
then $ABC$ and $A_1B_1C_1$ are perspective.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that $A,\,B,\,C$ are on $\mathcal{C}$. Applying Pascal theorem to the hexagon $AABBCC$, we obtain the perspectrix of $ABC$ and $A_1B_1C_1$. 

Without loss of generality, we may assume that $A\notin\mathcal{C}$. Set $BB_1\cap CC_1=P$, and let $B_1C_1$ intersect lines $BC,\,CA,\,AB,\,AP$ at $D,\,E,\,F,\,Q$, respectively, then
$$
(D,Q;B_1,C_1)\mathop{=}\limits^{P}(D,AP\cap BC;B,C)\mathop{=}\limits^{A}(D,Q;F,E)=(Q,D;E,F)
$$
i.e. $(D,Q),\,(B_1,E),\,(C_1,F)$ is an involution.

Note that $B_1,E$ are conjugate, and $C_1,F$ are conjugate (with respect to $\mathcal{C}$), so the involution is the one induced by $\mathcal{C}$, i.e. $Q, D$ are conjugate with respect to $\mathcal{C}$, and 
$$
Q\in\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(D)=\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(B_1C_1)\cap \mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(BC)=AA_1
$$
We see that $AA_1\cap B_1C_1=Q$, i.e. $A,A_1,P$ are collinear.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
In the beginning of the proof of @thm-poleperspective, we showed that $(D,Q),\,(B_1,E),\,(C_1,F)$ is an involution. This follows directly from Desargues involution theorem, which we will see later.
:::

## Dual Conics

Observe that conics are subsets of $\mathbb{P}$. Correspondingly, there are dual conics in $\mathbb{L}$, that is, subsets $\mathcal{E}\subset\mathbb{L}$ such that any six lines $m,n,\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4$ in $\mathcal{E}$ satisfy 
$$
m(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)=n(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)
$$ 
We temporarily call this the Brianchon condition.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
A nonempty set $\mathcal{E}\subset\mathbb{L}$ is called a (nondegenerate) dual conic if

(1) No three lines in $\mathcal{E}$ are concurrent.

(2) Any six-line set in $\mathcal{E}$ satisfies the Brianchon condition.

(3) For any $\ell\in\mathcal{E}$, there exists a unique point $P$ on $\ell$ such that
$$
\mathbb{L}_P\cap\mathcal{E}=\{\ell\}
$$
The point $P$ is called the tangent point of $\ell$ to $\mathcal{E}$. This implies that for any other point on $\ell$, there is a second line in $\mathcal{E}$ through it.

For any four lines $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4\in \mathcal{E}$, define their cross ratio to be
$$
(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)_\mathcal{E}=m(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)
$$
where $m$ is an arbitrary line in $\mathcal{E}$.
:::

We may define the polar transformation with respect to a dual conic. However, the polar transformation $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{E}}$ with respect to the dual conic $\mathcal{E}$ is also a dual transformation such that $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{E}}\circ \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{E}}$ is the identity. This suggests that there is a correspondence between conics and dual conics. Note that polar transformations realize duality, so the polar transformation takes a conic to a dual conic, i.e. 
$$
\mathcal{E}_1=\{\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(X)\mid X\in \mathcal{C}_1\}
$$
is a dual conic.

::: {#thm-dualconic}
The set $\mathcal{E}\subset\mathbb{L}$ is a dual conic if and only if $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of all tangents of some conic. Dually, a subset in $\mathbb{P}$ is a conic if and only if it is the set of tangent points of some dual conic.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Note that the polar transformation with respect to a conic $\mathcal{C}$ takes $\mathcal{C}$ to the set of tangents of $\mathcal{C}$, so the set of tangents of a conic is a dual conic. Dually, the set of tangent points of a dual conic is a conic. Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a dual conic, and $\mathcal{C}$ be its set of tangent points. It suffices to show that the set of tangents of $\mathcal{C}$ is $\mathcal{E}$.

Given $\ell\in\mathcal{E}$, suppose that $\ell$ passes through $Q\in\mathcal{C}$, and $Q$ is the tangent point of $m\in\mathcal{E}$. From the definition of tangent points, $m=\ell$, i.e. $\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}$ intersect at the tangent point of $\ell$ to $\mathcal{E}$, so $\ell$ is tangent to $\mathcal{C}$. Conversely, if $\ell\notin\mathcal{E}$, then there are two distinct tangent points of $\mathcal{E}$ on $\ell$ (the dual of this is that there are two distinct tangents through a point not on the conic), i.e. $\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are not tangent. This shows that the set of tangents of $\mathcal{C}$ is $\mathcal{E}$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The set of tangents $\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{C}$ of the conic $\mathcal{C}$ is called the **envelope** of $\mathcal{C}$. In the same manner, the set of tangent points $\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{E}$ of the dual conic $\mathcal{E}$ is called the envelope of $\mathcal{E}$. From the proof of @thm-dualconic, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{C}}=\mathcal{C}$. Usually we denote the cross ratio on the envelope of a conic by
$$
(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)_\mathcal{C}:=(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)_{\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{C}}
$$
:::

In conclusion, there is a 1-1 correspondence between conics and dual conics: conics and their envelopes (and dually, dual conics and their envelopes). In fact, the polar transformations with respect to $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$ are the same.

::: {#lem-dualpolar}
The polar transformations of a conic $\mathcal{C}$ and its envelope $\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{C}$ are the same. Dually, the polar transformations of the dual conic $\mathcal{E}$ and its envelope $\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{E}$ are the same.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
It suffices to show that $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}$ and $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}}$ agree on $\mathcal{C}$ (since they are dual transformations, we check for four noncollinear points), which follows the previous arguments.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
For historical reasons, an element in $\mathbb{L}$ is viewed as a subset of $\mathbb{P}$, so it is not easy to visualize a dual conic. Usually we think of it as the envelope of some conic, and sometimes identify $\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{C}$, for example, the cross ratio on $\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{C}$ would be written as the cross ratio on $\mathcal{C}$. The notation $\mathcal{E}$ for dual conics stands for "envelope".
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Example.**
Suppose that $\{\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(X)\mid X\in \mathcal{C}_1\}=\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}_2}$, then we write $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{C}_1)=\mathcal{C}_2$ for short.
:::

::: {#thm-brianchon}
## Brianchon
Given six lines $AB,BC,CD,DE,EF,FA$ (no three of which are concurrent), then these six lines are on the same dual conic (i.e. tangent to the same conic) if and only if $AD,BE,CF$ are concurrent. By abuse of language, we also say that the six lines are conconic.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This is the dual of Pascal theorem.
:::



::: {#thm-dualsteiner}
## Dual of Steiner conic
Let $\ell,m$ be distinct lines, and $f:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to \mathbb{P}_m$ be a projective map.

(1) If $f(\ell\cap m)=m\cap \ell$, then there exists a point $Q$ such that $P,f(P),Q$ are collinear for each $P\in\mathbb{P}_\ell$.

(2) If $f(\ell\cap m)\neq m\cap \ell$, then the locus of $Pf(P)$ (where $P\in \mathbb{P}_{\ell}$) is a dual conic containing $\ell,m$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This is the dual of Steiner Conic.
:::

## A Generalization of Steiner Conic

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic and $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$ be a projective map. From @cor-conicinvolution, $f$ is an involution if and only if there exists a point $P\notin\mathcal{C}$ such that $f$ is the map sending $X$ to the second intersection of $XP$ and $\mathcal{C}$.

::: {#thm-autenvelope}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic, $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$ be a projective map.

(1) If $f$ is an involution, then $Xf(X)$ passes through a fixed point independent of $X\in \mathcal{C}$ (in this case, $X\mapsto Xf(X)$ is not a projective map).

(2) If $f$ is not an involution, then the locus of $Xf(X)$ is a dual conic, and $X\mapsto Xf(X)$ is a projective map ($X\in \mathcal{C}$).

Dually, the locus of the pole of $Xf(X)$ is a line or a conic.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
We have shown the case where $f$ is an involution. When $f$ is the identity, the locus of $Xf(X)$ is the envelope of $\mathcal{C}$. We may assume that $f$ is neither an involution nor the identity. Let $\ell$ be the projective axis of $f$.

Let $A$ be a point on $\mathcal{C}$ satisfying $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(Af(A))\notin \ell$ (since $f$ is not an involution). Set
$$
Af(A)\cap Xf(X)=P,\,Af(X)\cap Xf(A)=Q
$$
By Brocard theorem, $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(P)$ passes through $Q$ and $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(Af(A))$, so
$$
X\mapsto f(A)X\mapsto \ell\cap f(A)X=Q\mapsto\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(Af(A))Q=\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(P)\mapsto P
$$
is projective.

Given $X_1,X_2,X_3\in\mathcal{C}$, set $Af(A)=\ell_A$ and $X_i f(X_i)=\ell_i$ for $i=1,2,3$, then
$$
(X_1,X_2;X_3,X)_\mathcal{C}=\ell_A(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,Xf(X))
$$
(since $X\mapsto P$ is projective). Replacing $A$ with another point $B\in \mathcal{C}$ such that $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(Bf(B))\notin \ell$, we get
$$
\ell_A(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,Xf(X))=(X_1,X_2;X_3,X)_\mathcal{C}=\ell_B(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,Xf(X))
$$
so the locus of $Xf(X)$ is a dual conic determined by the lines $Af(A),Bf(B),\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$, and $X\mapsto Xf(X)$ is projective.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
The dual of Steiner conic is the special case of @thm-autenvelope where $\mathcal{C}$ degenerates to two lines.
:::

There is another way to view @thm-autenvelope.

::: {#lem-alternativeenvelope}
Let $P$ be a point on a conic $\mathcal{C}$, $\ell$ be a line through $P$. Assume that $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{P}_\ell$ is a projective map such that $f(P)=P$. Let $Xf(X)$ and $\mathcal{C}$ intersect again at $X_1$, then as $X$ varies on $\mathcal{C}$, either $X_1$ is a fixed point or $X\mapsto X_1$ is a projective map.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $\ell$ intersect $\mathcal{C}$ again at $Q$. Fix $S,T\in \mathcal{C}$ distinct from $P,Q$, and let $S_1,\,T_1$ be the second intersection of $\mathcal{C}$ and $Sf(S),\,Tf(T)$, respectively. Suppose that $S_1=T_1=A$, then by the projective map method, $f(X)=AX\cap \ell$. Suppose that $S_1\neq T_1$. Define the projective map
$$
g:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C},\, g(S)=S_1,\,g(T)=T_1,\, g(Q)=P
$$
Since $g$ is not an involution, from @thm-autenvelope, the locus of $Xg(X)$ is a dual conic $\mathcal{E}$ containing $\ell$. We see that $f':X\mapsto Xg(X)\cap \ell$ is a projective map, so $f(X)=f'(X)$ by the projective map method (check $X=P,\,S,\,T$). The function $X\mapsto X_1$ is the projective map $g$.
:::

In @lem-alternativeenvelope, either $Xf(X)$ passes through a fixed point or the locus of $Xf(X)$ is a dual conic. Taking the polar transformation with respect to $\mathcal{C}$, then the locus of the pole of $Xf(X)$ is a line or a conic.

::: {#cor-dualenvelope}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic, $\ell$ be a line tangent to $\mathcal{C}$ at $P$. Fix a point $Q$ on $\ell$, and let $f:\mathcal{C}\mapsto \mathbb{L}_Q$ be a projective map such that $f(P)=QP$, then the locus of $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\cap f(X)$ is a line or a conic as $X$ varies on $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

Combining @cor-dualenvelope and Steiner conic, we obtain the following example.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Example.**
Let $\ell$ be a line, and $m,\,m_1,\,m_2$ be three distinct lines. Suppose that the functions
$$
f_1:\mathbb{P}_m\to\mathbb{P}_{m_1}, \,f_2:\mathbb{P}_m\to\mathbb{P}_{m_2}
$$
are projective maps such that
$$
X\in\ell\iff f_1(X)\in\ell\iff f_2(X)\in \ell
$$
Fix $P\in\ell$, then the locus of $PX\cap f_1(X)f_2(X)$ is a line or a conic as $X$ varies on $m$.
:::

## Dual Transformations

We have defined the concept of dual transformations in an earlier remark. We state the definition again.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Suppose that the function $\mathfrak{p}:\mathbb{P}\to \mathbb{L}$ satisfies

(1) If $P,Q,R$ are collinear, then $\mathfrak{p}(P),\mathfrak{p}(Q),\mathfrak{p}(R)$ are concurrent.

(2) If $P,Q,R,S$ are collinear, then 
$$
(P,Q;R,S)=(\mathfrak{p}(P),\mathfrak{p}(Q);\mathfrak{p}(R),\mathfrak{p}(S))
$$

(from (2), $\mathfrak{p}$ is bijective), then $\mathfrak{p}$ is said to be a **dual transformation**. The function $\mathfrak{p}$ gives rise to a function $\mathfrak{p}:\mathbb{L}\to \mathbb{P}$ satisfying 
$$
(P,\ell)\in \mathcal{I}\iff (\mathfrak{p}(\ell),\mathfrak{p}(P))\in \mathcal{I}
$$
The function $\mathfrak{p}\circ\mathfrak{p}$ is a projective transformation, which is denoted by $\mathfrak{p}^2$. 

For a dual transformation $\mathfrak{p}$, define the sets
$$
\mathbb{P}_{\mathfrak{p}}=\{P\mid P\in \mathfrak{p}(P)\},\,\mathbb{L}_\mathfrak{p}=\{\ell\mid \mathfrak{p}(\ell)\in \ell\}
$$
Suppose that $P\in \mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$, then $\mathfrak{p}(P)\in \mathbb{L}_\mathfrak{p}$, and $\mathfrak{p}^2(P)\in \mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$. If there exists a line $\ell$ such that $\mathbb{P}_\ell\subset \mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$, then $\mathfrak{p}$ is said to be a degenerate dual transformation (in this case, $\mathfrak{p}(\mathbb{P}_\ell)\subset \mathbb{L}_\mathfrak{p}$, i.e. we may also define degeneracy of $\mathfrak{p}$ from the set $\mathbb{L}_\mathfrak{p}$).
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
When $\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}$ is a polar transformation, then $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}=\mathcal{C}$. In general, $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ satisfies the following

(1) Let $\ell$ be a line. Suppose that $\mathbb{P}_\ell\cap \mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is empty. Let $P=\mathfrak{p}(\ell)$, then $P\notin\ell$ (otherwise $\ell\in \mathbb{L}_\mathfrak{p}$, $P\in \mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$). For $X\in \ell$, $\mathfrak{p}(X)$ passes through $P$. Define the projective map 
$$
f_\ell:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to \mathbb{P}_\ell,\,X\mapsto \mathfrak{p}(X)\cap \ell
$$
then the fixed points of $f_\ell$ are in $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$, contradiction. In conclusion, for any line $\ell$,  $\mathbb{P}_{\ell}\cap \mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is nonempty.

(2) Suppose that there are three collinear points $X_1,X_2,X_3\in \mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ (collinear on line $\ell$), then $\mathfrak{p}(X_i)$ passes through $X_i$ and $P=\mathfrak{p}(\ell)$. Since $\mathfrak{p}$ is bijective, $P\notin\ell$. From the projective map method, for $X\in \ell$, $\mathfrak{p}(X)=PX$, i.e. $\mathfrak{p}$ is degenerate. In conclusion, if $\mathfrak{p}$ is nondegenerate, then for any line $\ell$, $\mathbb{P}_{\ell}\cap \mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ consists of $1$ or $2$ points.

(3) Suppose that there exists a line $\ell$ such that $\mathbb{P}_\ell\subset\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$. Let $P=\mathfrak{p}(\ell)\notin \mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$. If $Y\in \mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is not on $\ell$, set $PY\cap \ell=X$, then $Y\in \mathfrak{p}(X),\mathfrak{p}(Y)$, so $Y\in \mathfrak{p}(P)$, i.e. 
$$
\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}=\ell\cup \mathfrak{p}^2(\ell)
$$
In conclusion, if $\mathfrak{p}$ is degenerate, then $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is either a line or the union of two lines, i.e. a degenerate conic.
:::

::: {#thm-nondegeneratedual}
Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a nondegenerate dual transformation, then $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is a conic.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Assume that $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is the identity. Fix three points $A,B,C\in\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$, and let
$$
\mathfrak{p}(BC)=A_1,\,\mathfrak{p}(CA)=B_1,\,\mathfrak{p}(AB)=C_1
$$
then the points $A,B,C$ are on the corresponding sides of $A_1B_1C_1$. Consider the involution 
$$
f:\mathbb{P}_{BC}\to \mathbb{P}_{BC},\,X\mapsto \mathfrak{p}(X)\cap BC
$$
then $f$ is the harmonic conjugate with respect to $B|C$, and $f(B_1C_1\cap BC)=AA_1\cap BC$, so
$$
(B,C;B_1C_1\cap BC,AA_1\cap BC)=-1=A_1(B,C;B_1C_1\cap BC,BB_1\cap CC_1)
$$
We see that $A_1,AA_1\cap BC,BB_1\cap CC_1$ are collinear, i.e. $A_1B_1C_1$ and $ABC$ are perspective. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the conic passing through $A,B,C$ and tangent to the three sides of $A_1B_1C_1$ (it exists from Pascal theorem on the hexagon $AABBCC$), then $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}=\mathfrak{p}$ (check the points $A,B,C,A_1,B_1,C_1$, and $BB_1\cap CC_1$), i.e. $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}=\mathcal{C}$.

Now we assume that $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is not the identity. Let $A,D\in \mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ be points such that
$$
A,\,B=\mathfrak{p}^2(A),\,C=\mathfrak{p}^2(B),\,D,\,E=\mathfrak{p}^2(D)
$$
are pairwise distinct (suppose that $A\neq B$ but $C=A$, then $\mathfrak{p}(A)=\mathfrak{p}(B)=AB$, contradiction, so the points $A,D$ exist). Let $\mathcal{C}=(ABCDE)$, and consider the projective map
$$
g:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C},\,g(A)=B,\,g(B)=C,\,g(D)=E
$$
From @thm-autenvelope, since $g$ is not an involution, the map
$$
h:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{E},\,X\mapsto Xg(X)
$$ 
is projective, where the dual conic $\mathcal{E}$ is the locus of $Xg(X)$. Let $\mathfrak{p}_h:\mathbb{P}\to \mathbb{L}$ be the extension of $h$ (the existence follows from the same argument as @thm-extension), i.e. for all $X\in \mathcal{C}$, $\mathfrak{p}_h(X)=h(X)$. Set $F=BC\cap DE$, then
$$
\mathfrak{p}_h(A)=AB=\mathfrak{p}(A),\mathfrak{p}_h(B)=BC=\mathfrak{p}(B),\mathfrak{p}_h(D)=DE=\mathfrak{p}(D),\mathfrak{p}_h(F)=CE=\mathfrak{p}(F)
$$
We see that $\mathfrak{p}_h=\mathfrak{p}$. Note that $\mathcal{C}\subset \mathbb{P}_{\mathfrak{p}_h}$, and for any $Q\in\mathbb{P}_{\mathfrak{p}_h}$, we may find two points in $\mathcal{C}$ collinear with $Q$. Since $\mathfrak{p}$ is nondegenerate, $Q\in \mathcal{C}$, i.e. $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}=\mathcal{C}$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
Suppose that the projective map $f:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C}$ is not an involution, then there exists a dual transformation $\mathfrak{p}$ such that $\mathfrak{p}^2=\rho$, where the projective transformation $\rho$ is the extension of $f$.
:::

::: {#lem-greatdegeneratedual}
Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a dual transformation such that $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is a single line, then $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is an involutive transformation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Set $P=\mathbb{L}_\mathfrak{p}$, $\ell=\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$. Let $X$ be any point and define $PX\cap \ell=Q$. Let $R\neq Q$ be a point on $\ell$, and set 
$$
\mathfrak{p}(X)\cap PR=Y,\,XY\cap \ell=Z,\,QY\cap PZ=W
$$
then
$$
\mathfrak{p}(X)=QY,\quad \mathfrak{p}(Y)=\mathfrak{p}(PR\cap XZ)=R\mathfrak{p}(XZ)=R(QY\cap PZ)=RW
$$
We conclude that $\mathfrak{p}^2(X)=\mathfrak{p}(Q)\cap \mathfrak{p}(Y)=PQ\cap RW$ is the harmonic conjugate of $X$ with respect to $P|Q$ (by @lem-cevaharmonic).
:::

::: {#thm-polarequiv}
Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a dual transformation, then $\mathfrak{p}$ is a polar transformation if and only if $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is the identity.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is the identity. If $\mathfrak{p}$ is nondegenerate, then from the proof of @thm-nondegeneratedual,  $\mathfrak{p}$ is the polar transformation with respect to $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$. Now suppose that $\mathfrak{p}$ is degenerate, then $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is a line or the union of two lines. If $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p} =\ell\cup m$ is a union of two lines, then $\mathfrak{p}^2(\ell)=m$, contradiction; if $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is a line, then we have a contradiction from @lem-greatdegeneratedual.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
Suppose that, unlike $\mathbb{C}^\times$, we cannot take the square root in the multiplicative group of the cross ratio, i.e. lines and conics may not intersect, then we may adopt the characterization in @thm-polarequiv as the definition of polar transformations (or even conics).
:::

## Degenerate Conics

A degenerate conic may be two distinct lines or two coincident lines (the latter is a further degeneration of the former). In the following, we will only discuss the case of two distinct lines.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Define the polarity with respect to $\ell_1\cup\ell_2$: let $\ell_1\cap\ell_2=P$, then two points $X,Y$ are said to be conjugate if $PY$ is the harmonic conjugate of $PX$ with respect to $\ell_1|\ell_2$. We use the convention that any point and $P$ are conjugate. The polar of a point $X$ is the set of all points $Y$ such that $X,Y$ are conjugate, so the polar of $P$ is the whole plane; the pole of a line $m$ is the set of points $Z$ such that $Z$ and $Y$ are conjugate for all $Y$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
The polar transformation with respect to $\ell_1\cup \ell_2$ is not a dual transformation, for the polar of $P$ is not a line. In later chapters, we will encounter the isoconjugate of a pencil of conics, in which the polarity of degenerate conics is needed. We will not consider the envelope of a degenerate conic since it is not a degenerate dual conic (i.e. two points).
:::

After defining the polarity, we define projective maps between degenerate conics: given degenerate conics $\ell_1\cup \ell_2$ and $m_1\cup m_2$, the function $f:\ell_1\cup \ell_2\to m_1\cup m_2$ is said to be a projective map if there are projective maps $f_1:\ell_1\to m_1$ and $f_2:\ell_2\to m_2$ (or $f_1:\ell_1\to m_2,\,f_2:\ell_2\to m_1$), such that $f_1(X)=f(X),\,f_2(Y)=f(Y)$ for all $X\in \ell_1,\,Y\in \ell_2$. We write $f=f_1\cup f_2$.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Corollary.**
There exists a unique extension of a projective map between degenerate conics to a projective transformation.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Let $\ell_1\cup \ell_2$ be a degenerate conic. Suppose that $f:\ell_1\cup \ell_2\to \ell_1\cup \ell_2$ is a projective map such that $f\circ f$ is the identity, and any three points in the fixed point set of $f$ are not collinear, then $f$ is said to be an involution on $\ell_1\cup\ell_2$.
:::

There are two types of an involution $f$:

(1) There exists $Q\notin\ell_1\cup\ell_2$ such that $Xf(X)$ pass through $Q$ for all $X\in \ell_1\cup \ell_2$. In this case, $Q$ is called the perspector of $f$.

(2) There exist involutions $f_1:\ell_1\to \ell_1,\,f_2:\ell_2\to \ell_2$ such that $f=f_1\cup f_2$. In this case, $f_1$ (resp. $f_2$) has a fixed point $R_1$ (resp. $R_2$) other than $\ell_1\cap \ell_2$. The line $R_1R_2$ is called the perspectrix of $f$.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
Similar to Brocard theorem, if $Q,R\notin \ell_1\cup \ell_2$ are conjugate, let the involution with perspector $Q,R$ on $\ell_1\cup \ell_2$ be $f_Q,f_R$, respectively, then $f_Q\circ f_R$ is an involution with perspectrix $QR$ (in the case of nondegenerate conics, it is also the involution with perspector $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(QR)$, but in the degenerate case, the pole of $QR$ is $\ell_1\cap \ell_2$, which does not give any information about the involution).
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic (possibly degenerate), and let $f:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C}$ be a projective map. Suppose that $f$ is a composition of finitely many involutions on $\mathcal{C}$, then $f$ is said to be an **inner automorphism** on $\mathcal{C}$. The set of all inner automorphisms on $\mathcal{C}$ is denoted by $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
An automorphism is a "suitable map" from an object to itself. In group theory, the inner automorphism of a group $G$ is the subgroup of the automorphism group of $G$ consisting of the conjugation automorphisms. I borrowed the term because I couldn't think of a better description, but as far as I know, there are barely any connections between the two concepts.
:::

If $\mathcal{C}$ is nondegenerate, then any projective map $f:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C}$ is an inner automorphism. We will show that this is not true when $\mathcal{C}$ is degenerate.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
The composition of two inner automorphisms is again an inner automorphism. This shows that $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})$ is a group.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Let $\mathcal{C}=\ell_1\cup \ell_2$ be degenerate, $P=\ell_1\cap \ell_2$. Define two types of $f=f_1\cup f_2:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C}$.

(1) Suppose that there exists fixed points $Q_1,Q_2$ such that 
$$
f_1:\ell_1\to \ell_2,\,X\mapsto Q_1X\cap \ell_2,\,f_2:\ell_2\to \ell_1,\,Y\mapsto Q_2Y\cap \ell_1
$$
and $P,Q_1,Q_2$ are collinear, then $f$ is said to be an **odd automorphism**.

(2) Let the fixed points of $f_1:\ell_1\to \ell_1$ be $P,X_0$, and let the fixed points of $f_2:\ell_2\to \ell_2$ be $P,Y_0$. Suppose that 
$$
(P,X_0;X,f_1(X))\cdot (P,Y_0;Y,f_2(Y))=1
$$ 
for all $X\in \ell_1,\,Y\in \ell_2$, then $f$ is said to be an **even automorphism**.
:::

The set of odd (resp. even) automorphisms is denoted by $\mathrm{Odd}(\mathcal{C})$ (resp. $\mathrm{Even}(\mathcal{C})$).

::: {#lem-classifyinn}
For a degenerate conic $\mathcal{C}=\ell_1\cup \ell_2$, 
$$
\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})=\mathrm{Odd}(\mathcal{C})\cup \mathrm{Even}(\mathcal{C})
$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
We will show the inclusion $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})\subset \mathrm{Odd}(\mathcal{C})\cup \mathrm{Even}(\mathcal{C})$ first. Note that an involution with a perspectrix is a composition of two involutions with perspectors. For $Q\notin\mathcal{C}$, let $f_Q$ be the involution with perspector $Q$. By induction, it suffices to show that the composition of $f_Q$ followed by a map in $\mathrm{Odd}(\mathcal{C})$ (resp. $\mathrm{Even}(\mathcal{C})$) is in $\mathrm{Even}(\mathcal{C})$ (resp. $\mathrm{Odd}(\mathcal{C})$).

Given $f=f_1\cup f_2\in \mathrm{Odd}(\mathcal{C})$, let $Q_1,Q_2$ be the fixed points associated to $f_1,f_2$, respectively, and let $g=f_Q\circ f$, then
$$
(P,Q_1Q\cap \ell_1;X,g(X))\mathop{=}\limits^{Q_1}(Q_1P\cap f_1(X)Q,Q;f_1(X),g(X))=(PQ_1,PQ;\ell_2,\ell_1)
$$
Similarly, $X_0=Q_1Q\cap \ell_1$ is a fixed point of $f_1$, $Y_0=Q_2Q\cap \ell_2$ is a fixed point of $f_2$, and
$$
(P,X_0;X,g(X))\cdot (P,Y_0;Y,g(Y))=(PQ_1,PQ;\ell_2,\ell_1)\cdot (PQ_2,PQ;\ell_1,\ell_2)=1
$$
i.e. $g\in \mathrm{Even}(\mathcal{C})$. The same argument shows that for $f\in \mathrm{Even}(\mathcal{C})$, $f_Q\circ f\in \mathrm{Odd}(\mathcal{C})$.

We have proven that $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})\subset \mathrm{Odd}(\mathcal{C})\cup \mathrm{Even}(\mathcal{C})$. Given $f\in \mathrm{Odd}(\mathcal{C})$, let $Q_1,Q_2$ be the fixed points associated to $f_1,f_2$, and let $Q\neq P$ be conjugate to both $Q_1$ and $Q_2$, then $g=f_Q\circ f$ is an involution on $\mathcal{C}$, i.e. $f=f_Q\circ g\in \mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})$ is a composition of involutions. Given $f\in \mathrm{Even}(\mathcal{C})$, then $f_Q\circ f\in \mathrm{Odd}(\mathcal{C})\subset \mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})$. Since $f_Q$ is an involution, $f\in \mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})$. We conclude that $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})=\mathrm{Odd}(\mathcal{C})\cup \mathrm{Even}(\mathcal{C})$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
From the classification in @lem-classifyinn, we see that when $f\in \mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})$, the projective axis $\ell$ of $f$ exists, i.e. for any $X,Y\in \mathcal{C}$, $Xf(Y)\cap Yf(X)\in \ell$. One may wonder whether it is possible to define inner automorphisms to be those projective maps with a projective axis. Regrettably, the projective axis exists when $f_1$ is the identity and $f_2$ has two fixed points, so this definition is not equivalent (and $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})$ wouldn't be a group).
:::

::: {#thm-innextension}
Let $\rho$ be a projective transformation. The following are equivalent.

(1) There exists a dual transformation $\mathfrak{p}$ such that $\mathfrak{p}^2=\rho$, or $\rho$ is a perspective transformation with its perspector on the perspectrix.

(2) There exists a (possibly degenerate) conic $\mathcal{C}$ and $f\in \mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})$ such that $\rho$ is the extension of $f$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a dual transformation.

Suppose that $\mathfrak{p}$ is nondegenerate. Set $\mathcal{C}=\mathbb{P}_{\mathfrak{p}}$, then $\mathfrak{p}^2(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{C}$, i.e. $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is the extension of a map in $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})$. 

Suppose that $\mathfrak{p}$ is degenerate, and $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is a single line, then from @lem-greatdegeneratedual, $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is an involutive transformation. Take any (nondegenerate) conic $\mathcal{C}$ such that the perspector of $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is the pole of its perspectrix, then $\mathfrak{p}^2(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{C}$, and $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is the extension of an involution on $\mathcal{C}$.

Suppose that $\mathfrak{p}$ is degenerate, and $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is the union of two lines $\ell_1\cup\ell_2$, then $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is the extension of a map in $\mathrm{Odd}(\ell_1\cup\ell_2)$ (since $\mathfrak{p}(\ell_1\cap\ell_2)$ passes through $\ell_1\cap\ell_2,\mathfrak{p}(\ell_1),\mathfrak{p}(\ell_2)$).

Suppose that $\rho$ is a perspective transformation with its perspector $P$ on the perspectrix. Take a degenerate conic $\ell_1\cup \ell_2$ such that $\ell_1\cap \ell_2=P$, then $\rho$ is the extension of a map in $\mathrm{Even}(\ell_1\cup \ell_2)$.

This shows that (1)$\implies$(2).

___ 

Conversely, let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic and $f\in \mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C})$ with extension $\rho$. 

Suppose that $f$ is an involution, then $\rho$ is an involutive transformation. Take a degenerate dual transformation $\mathfrak{p}$ such that $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is the perspectrix of $\rho$, and $\mathbb{L}_\mathfrak{p}$ is the perspector of $\rho$, then $\mathfrak{p}^2=\rho$. In the following, we assume that $f$ is not an involution.

Suppose that $\mathcal{C}$ is nondegenerate. Consider $g:X\mapsto Xf(X)$, and let the extension of $g$ be $\mathfrak{p}$, then $\mathfrak{p}^2=\rho$.

Suppose that $\mathcal{C}=\ell_1\cup \ell_2$ is degenerate, and $f$ is in $\mathrm{Odd}(\ell_1\cup \ell_2)$. Consider $g:X\mapsto Xf(X)$ (this is a projective map from a degenerate conic to a degenerate dual conic). Let the extension of $g$ be $\mathfrak{p}$, then $\mathfrak{p}^2=\rho$.

Suppose that $\mathcal{C}=\ell_1\cup \ell_2$ is degenerate, and $f$ is in $\mathrm{Even}(\ell_1\cup \ell_2)$. Set $P=\ell_1\cap \ell_2$. Let the fixed points of $f_1:\ell_1\to \ell_1$ be $P,X_0$, and let the fixed points of $f_2:\ell_2\to \ell_2$ be $P,Y_0$. When $X_0=Y_0=P$, $\rho$ is a perspective transformation with its perspector on the perspectrix. When $X_0\neq P$ and $Y_0\neq P$, take any nondegenerate conic $\mathcal{C}_1$ that is tangent to $\ell_1,\,\ell_2$ at $X_0,\,Y_0$, respectively. For $Q\in \mathcal{C}_1$, let $X_0Q\cap \ell_2=Y$, $Y_0Q\cap \ell_1=X$, then $f_2(Y)=X_0\rho(Q)\cap \ell_2$, 
$$
X_0(P,Y_0;Q,\rho(Q))=(P,Y_0;Y,f_2(Y))=(X_0,P;X,f_1(X))=Y_0(X_0,P;Q,\rho(Q))
$$
(this follows from the definition of $\mathrm{Even}(\ell_1\cup \ell_2)$), i.e. $\rho(Q)\in \mathcal{C}_1$. We see that $\rho$ is the extension of a map in $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{C}_1)$. From the previous arguments for nondegenerate conics, there exists a dual transformation $\mathfrak{p}$ such that $\mathfrak{p}^2=\rho$.

This shows that (2)$\implies$(1).
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
From the proof of @thm-innextension, we see that some projective transformations are not the extension of inner automorphisms.
:::
